The expedition left the coast in early spring, when the snow on the lower passes had started to melt but the rivers were not yet too high to cross. There were eleven of them: six surveyors, three porters who knew the valleys, a cook, and a young doctor who had never been further from the city than the seaside town where her parents spent their summers.

For the first week the work was slow but simple. Each morning the surveyors climbed to a high point, set up their instruments and took bearings on the peaks around them, while the porters moved the camp a few miles further along the valley floor. In the evenings they compared notes by the fire and redrew the rough map they had brought with them, which turned out to be wrong in almost every detail. Rivers ran in the wrong direction, a lake appeared where the map showed a forest, and one mountain that the old chart marked as the highest in the range was clearly lower than its neighbours.

On the ninth day the weather changed. A grey wall of cloud came over the ridge in the afternoon and by nightfall it was snowing hard. The porters said the storm would pass in a day, perhaps two, and that the safest thing was to stay where they were. The leader of the expedition, a stubborn man who had promised the ministry a finished map by the end of the summer, did not want to lose the time. Electric cars are often described as simple machines compared with cars that burn fuel. An electric motor has one main moving part, needs no oil changes, and delivers its full pulling force from the moment it starts turning. There is no gearbox in the usual sense, no exhaust system and no spark plugs. For the owner, this means fewer visits to the workshop and lower running costs.

The battery is where the complexity has moved. A modern pack is made of thousands of individual cells, each of which has to be kept within a narrow range of temperature and charge. A control system measures every group of cells many times a second, balances them against each other, and decides how much power the car may draw or accept at any moment. On a cold morning it may warm the pack before allowing fast charging; on a hot day it may run pumps and fans to carry heat away.

Battery chemistry is also a matter of trade-offs. Some chemistries store more energy for their weight, which gives a longer range, but they rely on materials that are expensive or difficult to mine responsibly. Others are cheaper and last for more charging cycles, but the car becomes heavier for the same range. Manufacturers increasingly offer different chemistries in different versions of the same model, so that buyers who drive short distances do not pay for range they will never use.

Learning to play a musical instrument as an adult is different from learning as a child, and not always in the ways people expect. Adults are usually better at understanding why an exercise matters, at planning their practice, and at noticing their own mistakes. What they often lack is patience with sounding bad, and the free hours that children have after school.

The first months on a string instrument are especially humbling. The bow skids, the notes are out of tune, and the left hand cramps after a few minutes. Many adult beginners respond by practising for long sessions on the weekend and not at all during the week. Teachers almost always recommend the opposite: short, focused practice every day, even if it is only fifteen minutes, because the hands learn through repetition and sleep, not through a single heroic effort.

It also helps to play with other people as early as possible. Community orchestras and informal groups are often happy to welcome beginners on the easier parts, and the experience of being one voice in a larger sound is motivating in a way that scales and exercises are not. Playing with others teaches listening, counting and recovering from mistakes without stopping, which are skills that solo practice rarely develops.

When a small software company decides to move its systems to the cloud, the technical work is usually the easy part. Copying databases, setting up servers and changing configuration files can all be planned in detail and tested in advance. The harder part is changing how people work, and it is the part that most migration plans leave out.

In the old setup, one or two engineers often knew every machine by name. They could tell from the sound of a fan that a disk was about to fail, and they fixed problems by logging in and changing things by hand. In the cloud, machines are created and destroyed automatically, and a change made by hand to one of them will simply disappear the next time it is replaced. Every change has to be written down as code, reviewed and applied in the same way each time. For engineers used to quick manual fixes, this can feel slow and bureaucratic at first.

Costs change shape too. Instead of buying hardware once every few years, the company now receives a bill every month, and that bill grows quietly whenever someone forgets to switch off a test system. Successful teams make the costs visible: they tag every resource with the project that owns it, review the bill together, and treat an unexpected increase as a bug to be investigated.
